Do not \\\\\"fix\\\\\" a migrated skill by editing the leftover skill copy; that edit does not reach\\\\n   the agents now reading the memory.\\\\n\\\\n## Hard Rules\\\\n\\\\n- Create and delete apply only to custom (USER) skills \\\\u2014 managed (LEARNED) skills cannot be created or deleted from Chat.\\\\n- To edit a managed skill\\'s content, use `update_skill`. Only proceed with creation if no existing skill is a good fit, or the user explicitly wants a new one.\\\\n2. **Gather requirements** \\\\u2014 purpose, instructions, and whether the skill needs reference files\\\\n   - A skill only needs SKILL.md if the instructions fit in one document\\\\n   - Add reference files when the skill needs: runbook templates, API reference docs, configuration examples, troubleshooting decision trees, or service-specific guides that would bloat SKILL.md\\\\n   - Organize reference files by purpose: `references/` for documentation, `assets/` for templates and config files\\\\n   - Keep SKILL.md focused on the workflow and decision logic; put detailed reference material in separate files that the agent loads on demand\\\\n2. **Generate SKILL.md** with valid YAML frontmatter and markdown body\\\\n3. **Call `create_skill`** with title, content, and optionally resources\\\\n   - `create_skill(title=\\\\\"...\\\\\", content=\\\\\"...\\\\\")`\\\\n   - If the skill needs reference files: `create_skill(title=\\\\\"...\\\\\", content=\\\\\"...\\\\\", resources={\\\\\"references/guide.md\\\\\": \\\\\"# Guide content\\\\\", \\\\\"references/examples.md\\\\\": \\\\\"# Examples\\\\\"})`\\\\n4. **Show the user what was created** \\\\u2014 mention the skill name, description, and key steps. Do not show the ID.\\\\n5. **Ask the user to confirm** \\\\u2014 Use `ask_user` to confirm activation:\\\\n   ```\\\\n   ask_user(\\\\n     question=\\\\\"Would you like me to activate this skill?\\\\\",\\\\n     options=[\\\\n       {\\\\\"label\\\\\": \\\\\"Activate\\\\\", \\\\\"description\\\\\": \\\\\"Make this skill available for use\\\\\"},\\\\n       {\\\\\"label\\\\\": \\\\\"Keep inactive\\\\\", \\\\\"description\\\\\": \\\\\"Save the skill but don\\'t activate it yet\\\\\"}\\\\n     ]\\\\n   )\\\\n   ```\\\\n6. **On confirmation** \\\\u2014 call `activate_skill` with the knowledge_item_id to make it live\\\\n7. **The skill is now available** \\\\u2014 `create_skill` returns the skill content in its response, so you already have the instructions. Do not call `ask_user` again after activation \\\\u2014 no follow-up menus.\\\\n\\\\n### Update a Skill\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to edit or update a skill:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Read current content** \\\\u2014 use `get_skill` to get the current SKILL.md content\\\\n2. **Apply changes** \\\\u2014 modify the content as requested\\\\n3. **Call `update_skill`** with the knowledge_item_id and updated content\\\\n   - `update_skill(knowledge_item_id=\\\\\"...\\\\\", content=\\\\\"...\\\\\")`\\\\n   - To add a resource file: `update_skill(knowledge_item_id=\\\\\"...\\\\\", content=\\\\\"...\\\\\", resource_mutations=[{\\\\\"path\\\\\": \\\\\"references/new.md\\\\\", \\\\\"action\\\\\": \\\\\"ADD\\\\\", \\\\\"file_content\\\\\": \\\\\"# New content\\\\\"}])`\\\\n   - To edit a resource file: `update_skill(..., resource_mutations=[{\\\\\"path\\\\\": \\\\\"references/guide.md\\\\\", \\\\\"action\\\\\": \\\\\"EDIT\\\\\", \\\\\"file_content\\\\\": \\\\\"# Updated content\\\\\"}])`\\\\n   - To delete a resource file: `update_skill(..., resource_mutations=[{\\\\\"path\\\\\": \\\\\"references/old.md\\\\\", \\\\\"action\\\\\": \\\\\"DELETE\\\\\"}])`\\\\n   - Multiple mutations can be combined in a single call\\\\n\\\\n### Edit a Managed Skill (LEARNED)\\\\n\\\\nManaged skills hold learned content, so a direct edit follows the **same durability rule as a learned memory store**: it is **transient** \\\\u2014 the DevOps Agent\\'s next regeneration overwrites it. Disabled skills remain in the agent space but are not loaded by agents\\\\n\\\\n### Change Agent Type\\\\n\\\\nWhen a user asks to change which agent types can use a skill:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Call `update_skill_agent_type`** with the knowledge_item_id and the desired agent_types list \\\\u2014 see the tool\\'s `agent_types` parameter for the accepted values\\\\n2. **Report** \\\\u2014 confirm the new agent type targeting\\\\n\\\\n## SKILL.md Format\\\\n\\\\nCreate a valid SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter and markdown body:\\\\n\\\\n```markdown\\\\n---\\\\nname: my-skill-name\\\\ndescription: Brief description of what this skill does. Be specific about when\\\\n  the agent should use this skill (minimum 100 characters recommended).\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Skill Title\\\\n\\\\nInstructions for the agent when this skill is activated.\\\\n\\\\n## When to Use\\\\n- Condition 1\\\\n- Condition 2\\\\n\\\\n## Steps\\\\n1. Step one\\\\n2. Step two\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n### Frontmatter Rules\\\\n- `name`: Required. Lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only (max 64 chars). Must not start or end with a hyphen. Example: `rds-throttling-investigation`\\\\n- `description`: Required. Brief explanation of when to use this skill (min 100 chars recommended, max 1024 chars).\\\\n\\\\n### Resource Files\\\\n\\\\nSkills can include reference files alongside SKILL.md. Reference files provide additional context the agent can load on demand. Use resource files when the skill needs supporting documentation, examples, API references, or other supplementary content.\\\\n\\\\n**Allowed file types:** `.md`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.xml`, `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.html`, `.htm`, `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.gif`, `.svg`, `.webp`, `.pdf`\\\\n\\\\n**Restrictions:**\\\\n- No script files (`.sh`, `.py`, `.js`, `.ts`, `.rb`, `.pl`, `.ps1`, `.bat`, `.cmd`, `.exe`)\\\\n- No `scripts/` directory\\\\n- No files with shebang (`#!`) content\\\\n- Maximum 100 files, 6 MB total\\\\n\\\\n## Example\\\\n\\\\nUser: \\\\\"Create a skill that helps investigate Lambda cold start issues\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n1. Misconfigured APF settings can result in dropped API Server requests and significant workload disruptions.\\n\\nOne other approach for preventing dropped requests is changing the default FlowSchemas or PriorityLevelConfigurations installed on EKS clusters. The API Server will automatically reconcile these objects back to their defaults if modified unless the following annotation on the objects is set to false:\\n\\n```\\n metadata:\\n annotations:\\n apf.kubernetes.io/autoupdate-spec: \\\"false\\\"\\n```\\n\\nAt a high-level, APF settings can be modified to either:\\n\\n* Allocate more inflight capacity to requests you care about.\\n* Isolate non-essential or expensive requests that can starve capacity for other request types.\\n\\nThis can be accomplished by either changing the default FlowSchemas and PriorityLevelConfigurations or by creating new objects of these types. Be aware that allocating more assuredConcurrencyShares to either existing PriorityLevelConfigurations or to new PriorityLevelConfigurations will cause the number of requests that can be handled by other buckets to be reduced as the overall limit will stay as 600 inflight per API Server.\\n\\nWhen making changes to APF defaults, these metrics should be monitored on a non-production cluster to ensure changing the settings do not cause unintended 429s:\\n\\n1. The metric for `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total` should be monitored for all FlowSchemas to ensure that no buckets start to drop requests.\\n2. The values for `apiserver_flowcontrol_nominal_limit_seats` and `apiserver_flowcontrol_current_executing_seats` should be compared to ensure that the concurrency in use is not at risk for breaching the limit for that priority level.\\n\\nOne common use-case for defining a new FlowSchema and PriorityLevelConfiguration is for isolation. Suppose we want to isolate long-running list\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/scale-control-plane.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Control Plane Monitoring\",\"context\":\"### Asymmetrical traffic patterns\\n\\nWhat if one API server [pod] was lightly loaded, and the other heavily loaded? If we averaged those two numbers together we might misinterpret what was happening. For example, here we have three API servers but all of the load is on one of these API servers. As a rule anything that has multiple servers such as etcd and API servers should be broken out when investing scale and performance issues.\\n\\nWith the move to API Priority and Fairness the total number of requests on the system is only one factor to check to see if the API server is oversubscribed. Since the system now works off a series of queues, we must look to see if any of these queues are full and if the traffic for that queue is getting dropped.\\n\\nLet\u2019s look at these queues with the following query:\\n\\n```\\nmax without(instance)(apiserver_flowcontrol_nominal_limit_seats{})\\n```\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nFor more information on how API A&F works please see the following best practices guide\\n\\nHere we see the seven different priority groups that come by default on the cluster\\n\\nNext we want to see what percentage of that priority group is being used, so that we can understand if a certain priority level is being saturated. Throttling requests in the workload-low level might be desirable, however drops in a leader election level would not be.\\n\\nThe API Priority and Fairness (APF) system has a number of complex options, some of those options can have unintended consequences. A common issue we see in the field is increasing the queue depth to the point it starts adding unnecessary latency. We can monitor this problem by using the `apiserver_flowcontrol_current_inqueue_request` metric. We can check for drops using the `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total`. These metrics will be a non-zero value if any bucket exceeds its concurrency.\\n\\nIncreasing the queue depth can make the API Server a significant source of latency and should be done with care. We recommend being judicious with the number of queues created. For example, the number of shares on a EKS system is 600, if we create too many queues, this can reduce the shares in important queues that need the throughput such as the leader-election queue or system queue. I don't have a skill in this agent space with a literal "FP6" label, but here's what the evidence actually requires before you can call this "API saturation":

**What must be verified first**

1. **Which priority level(s) were throttled, not just that 429s occurred.** AWS's own control-plane monitoring guidance is explicit: *"Throttling requests in the `workload-low` level might be desirable, however drops in a `leader-election` level would not be."* Since this burst was isolated to `workload-low`, that's the level the API Priority and Fairness (APF) system is *designed* to shed first — it's not evidence the API server itself is under stress.
2. **Whether other, higher-importance levels also dropped requests** — check `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total` broken out by FlowSchema/priority level for `workload-high`, `leader-election`, and `system`. If those stayed at zero, the API server protected the traffic that matters and did its job.
3. **Seat/concurrency utilization vs. the nominal limit** — compare `apiserver_flowcontrol_current_executing_seats` (or `apiserver_flowcontrol_current_inqueue_request`) against `apiserver_flowcontrol_nominal_limit_seats` for `workload-low` specifically, not an aggregate total-requests number across all API server replicas (per-replica skew can make an averaged number look fine while one replica is actually saturated).
4. **Correlation with the rollout mechanics** — a deployment rollout typically causes a burst of LIST/WATCH reconnects, controller resyncs, and readiness/eviction churn, which is exactly the kind of bursty, low-priority traffic `workload-low` is built to absorb. A 3-minute, self-resolving window lines up with that expected pattern rather than sustained resource exhaustion.
5. **Actual control-plane health signals** — API server CPU/latency and etcd latency during the window. If those are normal, there's no corroborating saturation signal outside the one queue.

**Does it justify scaling the control plane?**

No, not on this evidence alone. A single-priority-level, 3-minute burst of 429s during a rollout is the textbook signature of APF correctly isolating non-essential traffic — not of overall API server capacity exhaustion. Also worth noting: EKS control plane scaling is automatic and AWS-managed, not something you scale directly; the available levers if this *were* a real problem are tuning APF's `assuredConcurrencyShares`/queue depth for `workload-low`, or reducing client-side request bursts (e.g., controller QPS/burst settings) — not "scaling the control plane."

If you want, I can look into pulling the actual `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total` breakdown for this cluster during that window to confirm no spillover into higher-priority levels.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
